title: The trunk with no tree
teaches: Prototaxites, an eight-metre fossil from the first land ecosystems, and how its identity has been argued from clues for over 165 years
summary: **Prototaxites was the tallest living thing on land about 400 million years ago.** Its trunks reached 8 metres when land plants were at most knee-high.
**Dawson named it as a rotted conifer in 1859.** Carruthers soon argued it was a giant seaweed.
**Its trunks are built of tangled tubes, not wood.** That ruled out a tree and pointed toward a fungus.
**Hueber argued in 2001 that it was a giant fungus.** The tubes came in three kinds, like those in a fungus's fruiting body.
**Its carbon suggested it did not make its own food.** Different trunks had different carbon make-up, as if each fed on different matter.
**Spore-bearing tubes were reported in one species in 2017.** That seemed to settle it as a fungus.
**In 2025 a chemical study argued it was not a fungus at all.** Its fossils lack the traces fungal walls leave, unlike true fungi in the same rock.
**The best answer now may be a lost branch of life.** Something that lived like a fungus, with no living relatives.

blocks.text: In 1843 the geologist William Logan, mapping the Gaspé peninsula of Quebec, found great fossil logs in the sea cliffs, some nearly a metre across, in rocks then thought to be far too old for trees, from before land plants had grown large. Sixteen years later the Canadian geologist John William Dawson described them. Under the microscope their cut faces showed long tubes, and Dawson took the tubes for the cells of wood that had rotted. He named the fossil ***Prototaxites***, first yew, believing it an early conifer.

The rocks are about 400 million years old, from the early part of the Devonian period, which ran from about 419 to 359 million years ago. More trunks have since been found on many continents, from about 430 to 370 million years ago. The largest stood about 8 metres tall. At the time the tallest land plants were small green stems a few centimetres to a few tens of centimetres high, with no leaves, no wood and no seeds. Prototaxites would have stood over them like a lighthouse.

blocks.caption: Prototaxites to scale, beside a person and the land plants of the early Devonian.

blocks.text: Dawson's tree did not last. In 1872 the British botanist William Carruthers looked at the same tubes and saw none of the features of wood: no rings, no pits, no cells joined end to end into water pipes. He argued that Prototaxites was a giant seaweed, like the kelps of today, and renamed it *Nematophycus*, thread seaweed. Dawson objected for the rest of his life, and the name Prototaxites survived, because by the rules of naming the first name given stands, even though the conifer did not.

The seaweed did not hold up either. Kelps live in the sea, and Prototaxites trunks are found in the rocks of ancient rivers and floodplains, alongside land plants. A seaweed of that size out of water would collapse under its own weight, and nothing about its tubes suggested a way to hold water against drying air.

For most of the twentieth century Prototaxites was left as a curiosity. In 2001 Francis Hueber of the Smithsonian Institution, after decades of cutting and examining specimens, published a long study of its anatomy. Its trunk was a dense mass of tubes of three kinds: wide tubes with thick walls, running lengthwise; thin branching tubes weaving between them; and thinner walled tubes branching and joining. Some tubes had cross walls with holes, like the pores of lesson 3. To Hueber this was the build of a fungus, a giant fruiting body packed into a trunk.

In 2007 Kevin Boyce, then at the University of Chicago, and his colleagues including Hueber tested a prediction. A plant or alga takes its carbon from the air, and all of them alive at one time carry much the same proportion of the two stable forms, or isotopes, of carbon: carbon-12 and carbon-13. An organism that eats instead carries the proportion of whatever it eats. They measured trunks from the same rock and found the proportion varied widely from trunk to trunk, more than in the plants around them. Prototaxites, they argued, did not make its own food; each trunk had lived on different matter in the soil, as a fungus would.[^carbon] Others suggested it might have been a giant lichen, a fungus with algae in its skin, which would have let it make some food of its own.[^lichen]

In 2017 Rosmarie Honegger and her colleagues described a small Prototaxites species from the Rhynie chert of Scotland,[^rhynie] preserved in such detail that its surface could be studied cell by cell. They reported layers of tubes holding spores, like the sacs of the sac fungi of lesson 6. If the small species and the giant trunks were the same kind of organism, as most assumed, it seemed settled: a giant fungus, from a time before trees.

In 2025 a team led by Corentin Loron and Sandy Hetherington at the University of Edinburgh went back to the Rhynie chert. The same rock holds undoubted fossil fungi, so Prototaxites could be compared with them side by side. They looked at the chemistry of the fossils with infrared light and other methods, searching for the chemical traces that chitin, the tough material of fungal walls from lesson 2, leaves as it breaks down. The true fungi in the chert had them. Prototaxites did not, and its chemistry looked like neither a fungus nor a plant. Its network of tubes also differed in detail from any fungus known.

They concluded that Prototaxites was a member of an extinct branch of complex life, unrelated to any group living today, which had arrived at a fungus-like body and way of feeding on its own, as the water moulds of lesson 2 did. Not everyone is convinced. Fossil chemistry after 400 million years is hard to read, and Honegger's spore tubes have to be explained. But the case for a fungus is weaker than it was.

blocks.caption: Four ideas about what Prototaxites was (the lichen idea is a kind of fungus), and the clues that bear on them.

events.label: William Logan finds fossil logs in the Gaspé cliffs
Dawson names Prototaxites, a rotted early conifer
Carruthers calls it a giant seaweed
Hueber argues it was a fungus
Boyce and colleagues: its carbon varies, so it ate rather than photosynthesised
Honegger and colleagues report spore sacs
Loron and colleagues: no fungal chemistry, a lost lineage

blocks.text: Whatever it was, Prototaxites shows how strange the first land ecosystems were. Before trees, the tallest thing on land was, on most views, not a plant, and it lived, as far as anyone can tell, by feeding on what the small plants and microbes around it left in the soil. The question of what it was has passed through at least four answers, each one put forward by careful people looking at real evidence, and each one replaced when new evidence came.

blocks.caption: Five questions on Prototaxites
blocks.task: Choose the best answer to each

items.ask: Why was Prototaxites so striking for its time?
choices: It stood up to 8 metres tall when land plants were ankle-high
It was the first animal on land
It was the first plant with seeds
items.why: In the early Devonian the tallest plants were small stems. Prototaxites trunks towered over them.

items.ask: Why did Carruthers reject Dawson's idea that it was a conifer?
choices: Its tubes had none of the features of wood
It was found in the sea
It had leaves like a fern
items.why: Wood has rings, pits and water pipes. Prototaxites was made of tangled tubes with none of those.

items.ask: What did the varying carbon in different trunks suggest?
choices: Each trunk fed on different matter instead of making its own food
The trunks grew in different climates
items.why: Photosynthesisers all take carbon from the same air. Organisms that eat carry the make-up of their food, which varies.

items.ask: Which clue argued against Prototaxites being a fungus?
choices: It lacked the chemical traces of chitin found in true fungi from the same rock
It made no spores of any kind
items.why: The 2025 study compared it with fungi preserved alongside it. They kept chitin traces; Prototaxites did not.

items.ask: What does 'a lost lineage' mean here?
choices: A branch of life with no living members that evolved a fungus-like way of life
A kind of fungus that is now rare
A seaweed that moved onto land
items.why: On the 2025 view, Prototaxites belonged to no group of living things alive today; like the water moulds, it arrived at a fungus-like life on its own.

carbon.title: Carbon-13
carbon.text: Carbon comes mostly as carbon-12, with about one per cent carbon-13. Photosynthesis takes up a little less carbon-13 than is in the air, by a fairly fixed amount, so plants of one time and place share a ratio. Prototaxites trunks differed from each other by more than plants did, as expected if each fed on a different mix of food.

rhynie.title: The Rhynie chert
rhynie.text: Near the village of Rhynie in Aberdeenshire, about 407 million years ago, hot springs flooded a marsh with silica-rich water, which turned plants, fungi, algae and tiny animals to stone, down to their cells. It is still the best window on early life on land.

lichen.title: A lichen?
lichen.text: The lichen idea, put forward by Marc-André Selosse in 2002 among others, has found little support: no layer of algae has been seen in the trunks. It would, though, have explained how so large a thing grew so big when the small plants around it left only a thin layer of dead matter to eat.
